📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One of the most prominent figures of the so-called Bluenami was not a candidate on the ballot, but rather a Twitch streamer and political commentator: Hasan Piker.

Sources indicate that this year Hasan was involved in dozens of races across the country, campaigning for progressive candidates like Michigan senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed. But you’re probably more likely to associate Hasan’s name with what other people have had to say about him—from Fox News commentators to more established members of the Democratic Party.

Industry observers note that hasan regularly courts controversy on both his hours-long Twitch streams, where he’s noted things like “America deserved 9/11,” and social media, where he’s written that Hamas “is a thousand times better than” Israel. He claims he’s often taken out of context, and that his audience knows what he really means—and where he stands. In his mind, he’s a leftist provocateur, maybe, but one who understands the importance of working-class values and electoral strategy.

It has been revealed that while Hasan has walked back some of his more inflammatory language, his rhetoric raises the question: Is he a liability to the cause he champions? Or is he successfully reaching the critical audience—namely, young men—that helped elect the wave of progressives poised to take office in January?

Industry observers note that with 2028 on the horizon, I wanted to know how Hasan thinks about his growing platform, and if he sees his role shifting in the media landscape. What responsibility does he have to his viewers and to the candidates he supports? And does he regret any of those past statements?

We also got into the DSA’s more extreme positions and how to make sense of them; why he thinks the Republicans put his thirst trap on the jumbotron at their convention; and how he, a self-proclaimed socialist, thinks about his own money.

Mark Guiducci: Hasan Piker, welcome to Fair Game.

Hasan Piker: Very excited to be here.

In a recent development, thanks for coming. Hasan, you are more online than just about anyone. You spend at least seven hours a day streaming. You reach tens of thousands of people at a time on average, and it’s all in the channel that you control. I’m curious, what are you doing here with me today? Why are you showing up for a show with a legacy media publication? What’s in it for you?

It has been revealed that well, I saw the clips and everybody looked really good. The lighting was perfect. I saw the Dari[aliza Avila Chevalier] clips, I saw Ta-Nehisi [Coates], and I was like, I got to get in on that.

Yeah. So shouts out to the team. You guys did a phenomenal job lighting this up. It looks very cool too.

Okay. We’ll take the compliment.

Recent findings suggest that but the serious answer is, I mean, I reach an audience that obviously does not watch television, does not read legacy publications at all. And I want to show people that read Vanity Fair that I am not a terrorist.

In a recent development, right. Which brings me to my next question because—.

Yeah, exactly. That would be the name of the episode. You’ve been everywhere this year, and you became this kind of bogeyman for the right, who probably have never heard you, watched your stream, or heard anything you’ve said out of your mouth. They’ve just heard quotes repeated by news anchors. And not even just for the right, even for some on the left. And you played this interesting role because you were a surrogate and a media figure and then a media figure covering the media as well. I want to spend a little bit of time talking about how you see your role. And to start, do you consider yourself a journalist?

It has been revealed that okay. Because it’s like you present this interesting latest type of figure. I was thinking about how you’ve done an interview with CNN, you’ve done interviews with MS NOW, but they don’t have you on as much as I would expect them to.

I have some thoughts, but I wonder why you think that is.

It has been revealed that I think I’ve pissed off a bunch of executives over there, because, in my experience, there are plenty of amazing reporters and journalists and producers that I know that work at all of these newsrooms, right? But from what I have seen, the masthead has a very different editorial slant than sometimes what the reporters want to cover.

Because they talk about you a lot.

They talk about me a lot. And also I’ve never been invited on any of these outlets as a pundit either, which is also strange because, as you also pointed to, I don’t just operate as a campaignster. As a matter of fact, that’s something I did very briefly and I did not like it at all. I’m first and foremost a commentator…. I do have the capacity to do journalism at times. I’ll do interviews with candidates. I’ll go out and—.

According to recent reports, well, candidates I like. Sometimes I do interviews with candidates I don’t like or I’m unsure about as well. The problem is most of the candidates don’t want to come on if they know I’m gonna cook ’em. Like Gavin Newsom, I have had feelers out to get him on the broadcast.

I have. Gavin, Gavin, come on the show. I am a taxpaying California resident. I’m one of your constituents. You want to be president in 2028, you’re gonna have to be able to talk to people like myself.

All right. So, Hasan, this cycle you were involved in some way in, by one count, 48 different candidates’ races, and AIPAC and pro-Israel groups spent about $101 million in those races. And on Election Day, your stream was the second most watched in the country after NBC News’s “Kornacki Cam.” With a little bit of distance, how are you thinking about what happened a couple of weeks ago, both for yourself and for the country?

Sources indicate that I feel a lot of hope. Hopefully it’s not going to be short-lived. But I feel very excited for the first time in a very long time, after 10 years of some of the most odious politics that we’ve seen from Trumpism, from MAGA. We finally saw a real sea change through electoralism. People truly have had enough with Trumpism.

Industry observers note that I wouldn’t be so certain because I feel like if there’s one controlled opposition party that is capable of breathing life back into MAGA, it would be the establishment Democrats. So I’m a little bit worried, but it’s very clear that people are truly fed up.

Recent findings suggest that all right. So there are a couple of different narratives that are coming out of the midterms right now. Rahm Emanuel, for instance, is touting this as a victory for moderate Democrats, saying that they ran 21 points above Kamala Harris. The DSA, meanwhile, is claiming that American voters have “emphatically endorsed socialism.” Other pundits are saying that these major gains have nothing to do with the Democrats and are actually about the war in Iran and high gas prices. So does this debate between moderates and progressives feel like a healthy back-and-forth to you, or does this feel like the upcoming aisle that has to be straddled?

Recent findings suggest that I mean, I think this is not even a new debate. This factional battle has existed within the Democratic Party and perhaps—.

Yeah, but the progressive wing was always really fringe.

Recent findings suggest that and now we’re talking about—I don’t know if 50/50 is right. I don’t want to use numbers, but—.

I think it’s a testament to our success, especially in the midterms, that there are a lot of people who are trying to protect their comfortable sinecures and are outright panicking. And all of that completely sidesteps the reality that the vulgar Bernie-ism of 2016 was echoed through every single candidacy, every single campaign all across the country, from the obvious Berniecrats like Abdul El-Sayed to even people like Roy Cooper, who in the past were very moderate, very centrist. And he still is a center-right figure, which clearly works in North Carolina. But even he was railing against data centers, billionaires, the uncertainty surrounding AI. I mean, this is left populism. And that rhetoric, one could say, was deployed in the past by even the likes of Bill Clinton and Al Gore.

Recent findings suggest that but for some strange reason, there was a turning point in 2016 where the Democratic Party adopted this strange role of defending the corporate class and defending the elites and took ownership over, I guess, defending these institutions overall. And these institutions are worthy of defending, for the record. However, from the perspective of the masses, if the government is failing them, if these institutions are failing them, then they wanted someone to break it. And that was obviously the right populism of Donald Trump. And break those institutions, he surely did. And we’ve seen the devastating results of that.

So you credit the progressivism with what happened on election night?

Industry observers note that absolutely. I mean, there’s certainly local moderation on concerns, right? Because James Talarico went from saying “God is nonbinary” to “we need to defend our transgender brothers and sisters, our neighbors,” which is, again, insanely woke for Texas, or just in general, right? There are far more conservative figures in the party than James Talarico’s current position on the trans problem.

Okay. But sometimes the way that you run—oftentimes the way that you run needs to be different than the way that you govern or lead once you’re there. Do you think it is productive to continue pushing some of the farther-left ideas once they get to Congress? Or is pragmatism and getting things done, you know, defining things that are really achievable and sticking to them as a bloc, as a group, and pushing them over the line— when you’re talking to some of these winners, are you talking about [that]?

I think if I could speak to the entire incoming freshman class or the entire caucus—.

Sources indicate that I would say, be bold, be brave, and obviously immediately implement accountability. Investigations are an absolute must. This is what people are demanding. After the economy, the second concern, the biggest concern, is corruption. The second term with Trump has been unbelievable. I mean, look, I’m Turkish. I’ve seen corruption in the Turkish government. I’ve seen corruption and tracked it and talked about it all around the world with different governments. I’ve never seen anything like what the Trump administration has done because of how flagrant and in your face it was. And I think people responded to that, finally, in the appropriate way they should, with anger.

So you’re calling for subpoenas and investigations.

I think impeachment, especially for Trump, is probably the last thing that I care about. I mean, I want these guys to go to jail. Let’s be clear. If they’ve done the crime, they need to do the time. I don’t think anyone is above the law. We have to restore law and order. So I’m a law-and-order Democrat. And I know that sounds something very different in Washington, DC, or in general. I think when politicians say that, they mean, like, punish the poor for minor crimes. I’m talking about punishing the wealthy for their corruption, for their major crimes, because they’re the ones who are robbing people blind.

But, you know, a lot of people would say that impeachment would be a distraction. So I guess what I’m saying is, if you had to choose three agenda items that the Democrats are agreeing on and they’re going forward with—you already said subpoenas and investigations.

Recent findings suggest that what else? What are the other two that in the first year you really want to see happen?

Recent findings suggest that I think it’s virtually impossible [with] the current DOJ to—they’re not impartial, right? I don’t think that we are going to move the needle on actual criminal investigations before the Democrats win the White House in 2028. But all of this is building up for that moment. And for that reason, I think we need to talk about affordability—and not just simply talk about affordability, but also explain how we’re going to solve the affordability crisis through a comprehensive legislative agenda. And one of the major issues around affordability that is oftentimes discussed as a separate thing, but it’s not, is health care. And the Democratic Party’s approach to health care has been lackluster. Even though Americans obviously overwhelmingly trust the Democrats with fixing health care or solving the problem with health care, the reality of the matter is, while the ACA was a fantastic improvement to what existed previously, it’s not enough, and we have to move the needle in a healthier direction. We have to push for a single-payer health care solution.

I’m perfectly fine with that. I’ve joked about that for years ’cause he’s so invested. He’s such a petty despot and so narcissistic that—.

Yes. I have pitched this over and over again on my show. Look, you win so big with Donald Trump if you go to Donald Trump and you say, “Look, Obamacare, not the best, right? Now you get to destroy Obamacare and you get to build something else in your name. We call it Trumpcare. It’s single-payer. It’s Medicare for All.” I think he would do it.

Recent findings suggest that look at this. Bipartisan collaboration.

Yes, I’m pragmatic. I’m bipartisan.

Sources indicate that all right, so let’s take a step back. You were talking a second ago about how Talarico was woke. And on November 4, Twitter, formerly known as X, was amazing. Memes, jokes, you know.

I see what you did there. Yeah. We flipped it back.

According to recent reports, yeah, we flipped it back. With the Democrats’ victory, the idea that woke was back, do you think that’s true? Do you think that we’re going to see, culturally, the return of this idea of woke? And do you think that’s a good thing for the Democrats?

It has been revealed that yes. I do think that the pendulum swing was an inevitability. I talked about this quite a bit. I saw the early warning signs when [Joe] Biden won. That was one of my major warnings that young men were going to go back to the Gamergate era of very far-right politics because the Biden administration was not delivering. And what ended up happening with this anti-woke narrative, this culture war that the Republicans had seemingly won, that they presented as a mandate, right, was some of the most odious commentary, some of the most vile rhetoric that anyone had ever seen.

In a recent development, definitely. The idea of woke now, though, I'm just curious—being politically correct or precise in one’s language was, for a time, an outward indication of being a progressive or maybe even being a good person in culture. Do you think that’s still the case?

I mean, I’m progressive, so I think so, but I’m a little biased. But I will say this: I think that there were certainly social excesses, which is ironic because this whole Woke 1.0, 2.0 distinction, I feel a little responsible for in the discourse because I jokingly used to say—.

Yeah, now I’ve joked about that too, and now journalists are reaching out to me being like, “Do you think Woke 3.0 is real?” I’m like, “I’m joking, guys. It’s not serious.” But here’s the thing, there is a little bit of sincerity there. I think one of the things that I routinely criticized during that 2016-to-2022, 2023, era of, I guess, Woke 1.0 was the social excesses, the maximalist demands, the inability to understand that people are complex and don’t have the same lived experience that everybody else has. I always would get so frustrated because we on the left say America’s a white supremacist country, and yet we don’t ever reflect on what kind of social conditioning comes along with that. So that if you do actually hear someone engage in a microaggression, for example, that we have to be a little bit more understanding and try to ease them into the conversation.

According to recent reports, and on the other side, people will say, “Oh, that’s normalizing this kind of behavior. It’s unacceptable.” And I totally see the other side of that argument as well, but I think, especially if you’re campaigning or especially if you’re building a movement, you do have to be a little bit more understanding and not be so hardheaded and assume that everyone has to agree with you from the jump without you making a convincing case as to why you might be correct.

Sources indicate that okay. All right. So we’ve talked a lot about what you think about the political landscape, but I want to talk also about your role in it right now and going forward. So initially, you were called the Joe Rogan of the left. Recently, you’ve mentioned you operate more like a Charlie Kirk. Is that the right analog for the kind of influence you want to have? And if not, is there another?

Recent findings suggest that I don’t think there is an appropriate analog because I’m everything all at once at the same time, because I work out and I do collaborations with people who are not expressly political, so that’s kind of like Joe Rogan. I go out and operate sometimes as a campaign surrogate, and I do rallies at college campuses and I deliver speeches, so that’s kind of like Charlie Kirk. But then usually my day-to-day commentary is what I like to jokingly refer to as a Rush Limbaugh for Zoomers. So I do all of those things at the same time, and that’s, I think, part of the reason why it’s so hard to make sense of what I do from the perspective of someone who just doesn’t understand Twitch or doesn’t understand exactly what I’m doing and has only seen negatively framed clips or clips out of context, that kind of thing. Having mentioned that, on the political-ideological side of things, of course I am the furthest from all of those figures. I’m just talking about the form and function of it all.

It has been revealed that okay. So it seems like you’ve been recently the guy that progressives come to when they’re trying to run a primary from the left, but then when they get to the general or to office, maybe they don’t need you as much, or they have left you behind, or they distanced themselves from you. And I think about [Zohran] Mamdani in this case. I just—.

Recent findings suggest that maybe because of that Rush Limbaugh–esque heightened rhetoric; do you agree with that characterization? And how does that make you feel?

Well, my feelings are immaterial in this. As long as they’re delivering, I think that’s what matters. I’ve stated this before: I love Zohran and, off the rip, my attitude on this was always just put the policies in the bag. If you’re delivering for the people of Newly introduced York, and if you’re delivering successfully and every success that you have as a democratic socialist mayor of New York bodes well for the rest of this movement, then I’m happy.

According to recent reports, yeah, but are you talking to him behind the scenes? There’s still a relationship there? Because honestly—.

Yes. But the thing is, what I’m doing is too upcoming for people to fully realize, to fully comprehend. So of course there’s going to be some growing pains as far as how to navigate through an unbelievably contentious media environment, especially if the candidate[s] themselves are Muslim. And, you know, I think that is the reason why—the two major figures that I can point to that have done a little bit of distancing, at least in rhetoric, even though they never disavow the platform, disavow the person, they just say, “Oh, I don’t agree with that statement”—those two figures are Abdul El-Sayed and Zohran Mamdani. They’re both very progressive. One’s a democratic socialist, the other one’s not, but they’re still very progressive for American politics, and they’re Muslim. I think that is a major part of the reason why I’ve given them a lot more bandwidth to operate in this space in whichever way they want to, because the expectation or the fears that they have are very real. As someone who has been at the center of a lot of this manufactured outrage, a lot of this controversy, being presented as an Islamist, jihadist at times, a terrorist, I know the role that the first Muslim senator has to play on the campaign trail. So on that front, of course they got to do what they got to do.

So you intellectually understand it, but do you feel used?

Recent findings suggest that I would only feel that way if they did not follow through on their promises that they made on the campaign trail. If Abdul came out tomorrow and was like, “Money out of politics? Maybe money in politics. Money in your pocket? Maybe you don’t get money in your pocket. Medicare for All? Medicare for some”—if he were to just flip the script on not just me, but Michiganders and America as a whole, then I would feel very betrayed.

It has been revealed that so we talked a little bit earlier about your audience at the very beginning. You know, you’re an interesting figure for them. There are a significant number of them that are with you for hours on end a day, and I think they probably look up to you. What responsibility do you feel to the people who watch your streams?

As far as the responsibilities that I have, I am very aware of them. I see myself as, in some respects, NPR for Zoomers. For many people, and now even an older audience as well, I am their primary news outlet. They have me on in the background, and I’m offering news and commentary throughout the day while they’re going through and doing their chores or at work with me blasting in one ear. So I know that if I were to stop randomly, people would feel it, because I see it as—I listen to The Daily; I listen to NPR every morning. If somehow I wake up one morning and NPR is no longer on, I’d be like, What happened? How am I gonna figure out what’s going on in the world?

Yeah, that’s just a lot of pressure, though, because NPR has a whole staff of people that, [if] someone’s sick, someone can pinch-hit.

According to recent reports, I mean, I’m fine living in that environment. I’m happy to do it. I’m happy to take on that responsibility.

Can I ask, what’s your personal life like right now? I mean, that is a lot of time on the air, and probably you have to read the news yourself too. So are you seeing friends a lot? Do you see your family a lot?

I keep my private life private for obvious reasons ’cause there are a lot of insane people out there. But yes, I do spend a good deal of time with friends and family. I have normie friends as well that are just completely removed from the world of politics and from the world of Hollywood, influencers, that kind of thing.

Yeah, no, they keep me grounded, for sure, and my family certainly does as well. I spend every waking moment that I’m not on camera doing things like that, you know, enjoying the finer things in life.

Do you think of yourself as a role model?

Industry observers note that in some respects, yes. I don’t think people should follow everything that I do to a T, but I definitely do see that. I recognize the responsibility that influencers have over so many people, and I try to put my best foot forward in an effort to cultivate a nicer space on the internet, one that is more productive for people. I try to urge people to go out and unionize in their workplaces, join the Democratic Socialists of America, but then also at the same time, I try to get them to go out and work out. I’m very open about my fitness journey, my health journey. And the same even goes for my presentation. I’ve gone through these different eras now on my broadcast. Right now we’re in the suit arc. And then I sometimes see that reflected in the crowd as well when I go out to these rallies. I start seeing people also wearing suits, which is a little strange to experience, but it’s not the worst thing, right?

I think that’s a good influence.

Recent findings suggest that yeah, I think that is a good influence. You’re rocking a nice suit yourself.

In a recent development, I bought this at a photo shoot for Days magazine. This stylist had pulled this and I loved it.

I literally was like, “I’m buying this from you.” And then since then, she’s been pulling stuff for me.

Sources indicate that can I ask, are you having fun? Because it seems like you are, but then what we were talking about before, with the way that you might feel abandoned—and especially the past few months, this cycle, has it been fun?

According to recent reports, no, it has not been fun. I don’t think it’s great to be called a terrorist and lied about and slandered endlessly with the hopes that this could potentially tank the Democratic Party’s chances of bringing about accountability to this fascist administration. I did not enjoy that.

And I certainly also did not enjoy the fact that I was kind of left out on my own a little bit, where—of course I got a lot of support from the movement, DSA, and the wonderful slate of candidates that we worked with, but I’ve never had institutional backing. And as a matter of fact, there was a lot of anxiety from the institution that is the Democratic Party. So all of its loyal servants were going on TV and being like, “He’s a horrible person who needs to go away,” over and over again. So that didn’t feel great. ’Cause there’s always negative polarization when Trump attacks someone and the Republicans attack someone, but if there isn’t any backing from the liberal side, even from a partisan perspective, then that complicates things. All of a sudden you’re like, Okay, well, who’s on my side now? I have nobody to push back.

You’re playing this game where you try to find the worst quotes that you can and frame them as negatively as you can, and then attack candidates that might not even know the context behind some of these words. Bernie was, I think, the best, ironically enough, at dealing with it when he was asked by Abby Phillip. He called me a radio man, which is funny. He’s been on the show, still doesn’t know what I do, which is fine. That’s unc, that’s grand-unc. But he basically said, “Look, everybody says silly things. I mean, he talks for thousands of hours. He’s a radio man. And not only does everybody say silly things, but ultimately there’s a reason why he has such a passionate fan base, because we agree on the broad spectrum of issues that he advocates for, and so do all of his fans. So to reduce someone to a couple of choice clips is obviously going to never give you the full picture.” I mean, he didn’t use all those words.

It’s not about being a person; it’s about being a cudgel, just something that you can use as a counterbalance.

It has been revealed that I don’t think liberals, and even the left broadly, [are] ready for how to deal with that because we’ve never really had a person like me in the past. I mean, the Republicans obviously have three to four decades of this, coming from William F. Buckley all the way to Rush Limbaugh and Charlie Kirk and numerous other far-right figures, that they know how to brush this aside. I mean, JD Vance, when asked about his affiliation with Tucker Carlson, will be like, “He’s my friend.” And that’s it. That’s that.

It has been revealed that okay. So you’re streaming most of the day, you’re reacting to news in real time, and just even by your own admission, you’ve mentioned some—I think you said “silly things.” I would say some pretty extreme things along the way.

And I know you’ve walked back past statements. “America deserved 9/11”—how many times have you heard that this season? Quote: “If you cared about Medicare fraud, you’d kill Rick Scott.” You’ve said things that you wish you had said differently. Do you regret anything that you’ve said? Because I think regret is different than “wish I said differently.”.

It has been revealed that it’s a tough one. I mean, look, I probably will regret things that I will say in the future as well. It’s virtually impossible for me not to say things—.

Industry observers note that yeah, it is, but it also isn’t because I have apologized and taken back some of the things that I’ve stated and apologized for how I worded or framed things. But do I regret it? I mean, I feel like I’m stronger as a consequence of all of those experiences at the same time, so I don’t know.

Do you feel like someone in your role has a different responsibility with their words or their public platform than an elected official or even a journalist?

Okay. But you also said that you are a role model.

Can you parse that a little bit?

Sources indicate that yeah, absolutely. It goes back to the space that I occupy and what I try to do with it. Right? I don’t think that I am, at least to my audience or anyone else that’s paying attention, doing anything that’s remotely politically as toxic as the way that the current systems operate. The rude behavior that I demonstrate is what people get frustrated by or what they attack, but—.

Yeah, I am vulgar, for sure. But I think the systems of violence and oppression that people are subjected to [are] far worse than any vulgar thing I could have ever said. And we kind of saw this dynamic play itself out on the campaign trail as well. And I think the finality of it all came with Haley Stevens, when she decided to lean into the “Hasan Piker is such a problem that I'm leaving the Democratic Party and endorsing the Republican platform.” [That] was, I think in some respects, a wake-up call because it forced everyone to go, Wait a minute. No, those guys are actually far worse. What are we talking about? Right? Because at the end of the day, Donald Trump is not only vulgar, but he’s also violent. And sure, I’m vulgar, but ultimately I’m fighting for social justice. I’m fighting for people who are dispossessed, people who don’t get heard at all. I’m trying to offer them a voice, a platform for their frustrations, and communicate their desires, their anxieties.

Do you think the vulgarity actually helps you with your audience? Because if they’re young men, men in their 20s, it’s like the edgelord vernacular.

Certainly, but I don’t do it for some tactical purpose. I do it because that’s just who I am.

In a recent development, I mean, I always say, look, if you go after marginalized people, vulnerable populations, and you bully them, I’m gonna bully you. Someone has to do it.

For what it’s worth, you’re being very civil right now.

In a recent development, oh yeah. I mean, this is a very different format. I am very different in these sorts of professional settings than I am on my own broadcast where I’m offering off-the-cuff commentary on these hot-button issues.

Is this more performative, or is that?

I would say this is more performative.

Recent findings suggest that I’m much more civil here. I’m not going to talk in the same way that I do on my broadcast. But here’s the thing, I can’t be fake on my broadcast. And I’m not even saying I’m being fake here. I’m just being nice.

But what I will say is this: A lot of people don’t realize that this is an interactive medium. Most people think, when they see a clip, especially if it’s chopped a certain way—.

It has been revealed that yes. Most people think this is my preproduced, prescripted statement ’cause that’s all they’ve seen from the Jake Tappers of the world. They don’t realize that I am offering extemporaneous commentary on a breaking news story in real time, without a production team, while simultaneously—.

Recent findings suggest that no. While simultaneously duking it out with anonymous accounts. What is the one thing that everybody hates on Twitter and everywhere else on the internet?

The comment section. My entire platform revolves around yelling at the comment section, and the comment section is yelling back at me.

We’ve got to get you a practice.

According to recent reports, but that is like, I’m in the zone. That’s when I’m in the pocket. I love being in that space.

You’ve been outspoken about distinguishing criticism of Israel from antisemitism, but do you think that there are moments when legitimate anger at Israel can create an environment in which antisemitism becomes acceptable, even among people who would never consider themselves antisemitic?

And what responsibility do you think you have, given the size of your audience and your influence with it, to call that out when it happens?

I do call it out when it happens, and it happens quite frequently. It’s not a secret that antisemitism has exploded in the Western world, especially after October 7. And that is why I take special care and consideration when talking about this concern in particular. Whenever I talk about Israel, there’s always going to be some people who will be like, “Well, you know how the Jews are.” And I will always take the time out to explain to my audience, and to whoever’s saying an offensive statement or an antisemitic statement, why they’re wrong. And I think it’s important to do that, not because—it’s not like the canary mission of the ADL is gonna be like, “This guy that we have presented to you as a prominent critic of Israel, that we’re desperately trying to paint as an antisemite, has actually spent thousands of hours combating antisemitism and will continue to do so because he’s an antifascist.” They don’t want to present the complexity of that argument because, let’s be real, it’s pretty tough trying to defend Israel. It’s not an easy endeavor.

Can you think of a time when you contributed to that problem, not intentionally, but maybe through something you stated and the way your audience responded?

No, because every clip that people post, or every moment that people have posted to point to this suspected antisemitism that I harbor, oftentimes is sandwiched between a comment that I have made leading up to it that completely destroys the narrative. The example I will present to you is the famous moment where I got disavowed by the entire Democratic Party. I said something that I have said as an anti-Zionist for the last decade and will continue to say because it’s the truth: that Jews are not monolithic and that Israel should not be the responsibility of the entire Jewish population, and that anti-Zionism is not antisemitism; however, that forced conflation of Jews in Israel is increasing antisemitism. And they chopped it up and packaged it and turned it into this major media moment.

According to recent reports, so speaking of misinterpretations, you recently filed a defamation lawsuit against conservative commentator Scott Jennings, although you’ve said you were very deliberately anti-litigation for a long time before that. So what changed? Why this suit? And who else are you planning to sue?

So what changed is the heinous nature of this defamation. It was definitely a bridge too far. I feel like there is a boundary that was crossed that I could no longer abide by. And there’s a level of defamation and slander that takes place in the political conversation, but what Scott Jennings did was so disgusting and so malicious that I had to demand a retraction. Snopes did an article immediately because it was so heinous. He claimed that I was on video advocating to lynch Black voters. I’ve spent my entire life fighting against white supremacy, and the fact that they maliciously edited this video to make it seem like I was in favor of something that I’ve always been in opposition to, something so heinous, a hate crime, was outright unacceptable. So I wish that it didn’t have to get to litigation, but for some strange reason, they decided not to respond to our request for a retraction and now we’re here.

Who else are you planning to sue?

I mean, there are a lot of people who have engaged in that exact same kind of defamation and slander. So whoever has participated in it should probably be on the lookout.

Okay. In the national chapter of the DSA, there are some pretty extreme platform positions that—I saw Mamdani answer these questions on Fox News the other night. I’m sure you did too.

And I'm actually just curious where you stand on some of them.

So here’s the thing with the platform in its entirety. I think the format itself doesn’t actually do justice to the program, to describe the program, and it’s almost impossible to explain it as an elected representative or a mayor in a hostile or contentious media environment, if you’re on Fox News or whatever. The glitch, I think, with the program is, there are certain elements of it that I don’t agree with fundamentally, but it’s a democratically organized, democratically voted-on program that DSA members voted for. And the way I see it is, these are very, very long-term goals, and I think this is not talked about in mainstream media at all. It is a platform, but it’s more so a North Star that we are working toward. Designing society in a way that yields egalitarian outcomes. That we do away with certain systems of cruelty is an honorable goal, is a just goal, even if I don’t fully agree with some elements of it.

I’m not a prison abolitionist; I’m not a police abolitionist. The reason why I don’t believe in that concept is because I think that these are necessary functions that must exist, but also must serve the people. Right now it doesn’t. It serves capital and that needs to change, that needs to be retooled. However, I also recognize that the current system that exists is far more ruthless, far more insane, even if we’ve normalized it, than even police abolition is. So from my perspective, if we look at where we’re at, the carceral state that exists, where America has 25% of the entire planet’s prisoner population despite only making up 4% of the overall population, and the recidivism rates that we have in this country, and the fact that we even have a private prison system in this country—that’s insane. That is insane by global standards. So it’s tough for me to sit here and say I oppose the DSA platform and program when I understand what they are trying to communicate.

In a recent development, and also, I think what is the regular order of business right now is far more insane than even prison abolition. Even though prison abolition is far-fetched and I don’t agree with it, I think the best possible way to go about it would be to have an electoral program, the perceivable, the permissible, the possible, and then the long-term goals, the long-term agenda, ’cause it’s not going to be easy to run and try to win on a platform that is not only idealistic, but also does not reflect the current societal understandings of concepts. Because most people think cops are awesome, they can do no wrong, they’re heroes, they’re constantly fighting crime, and they’re stopping rapes from happening, and they’re diving in front of bullets, but that’s not the case. I wish that was the case, but that’s not the case. But people overall [have] a very positive attitude about policing as an institution.

According to recent reports, but there’s also quick and quippy ways to respond fast. I just told you I’m a law-and-order Democrat, right?

Immediately that signals something. Another thing that I always say about policing is, I want police to do their jobs. I think that, by and large, they have a profoundly important task that they have to accomplish. Their presence is supposed to invoke law and order. Their presence sometimes invokes lawlessness and disorder. That’s unacceptable. They’re very well paid. They have the best unions. Do your jobs better. That’s my attitude on policing. So it’s antagonistic, but it’s also a demand that I’m making from this institution that I truly do believe is important for society to function. That’s one way to tackle this issue in a way that Americans understand. I like to call it chudifying your commentary. Zohran does a very good job of libifying his commentary. He’s very liberal-appealing. I like to do the opposite. I like to chudify it. I appeal to the chuds. I speak from that tone and that language when I advocate for certain things.

Yeah, edgelord vernacular, sure. But it’s kind of like, whether we’re talking about abortions or whether we’re talking about transgender bills, like anti-trans bills, I’m like, I don’t want the fucking government getting involved in these affairs. What do you want? You want some creepy pervert to do penis inspection day at your high school? What are you, a pervert? Are you a pedophile? I want small government when it comes to this kind of stuff. And that is a way to argue from a perspective that I think right-wingers can understand.

In a recent development, switching gears, we talked a little bit about suits for a second, but I want to talk about style more largely. So at the RNC’s midterm convention in September, there was a 25-foot selfie of you in underwear displayed on the jumbotron. How do you think about that?

It’s a strange thing because I wish I was as in shape right now as I was, because that was peak.

Recent findings suggest that thank you. But also at the same time, I’m like, Oh, I wish I looked like that right now.

Why do you think they’re so obsessed with your looks? What is going on there? How is that helpful to them actually?

It’s not. I think about that quite a bit. I think…they’re gay.

Sources indicate that that’s it. I think they’re in the closet. There are a lot of Republican operatives that are just either gay or in the closet and haven’t been able to figure out how to communicate their desires. So they were just frustrated and confused. But there’s no other reason to have this pathological, this psychosexual, obsession where you’re like, “My opponent, this political opponent, is a dangerous guy. He’s a radical communist, Islamist, jihadist.”.

In a recent development, “And he’s also sexy. Look at him shirtless. Look at him shirtless.” Because I thought these guys were peak masculinity. I thought that’s what they were about. The Joe Rogan Experience, you know, Brazilian jiujitsu, and working out was supposed to be the thing in the right.

There’s nothing unmasculine about being gay.

I’m kidding. That’s not how they think of it. I know.

And not only that, but also, ultimately, why are they showing a shirtless photo of me where I look jacked?

Recent findings suggest that yeah. Okay. But it’s not just the GOP. Almost any coverage of you, including now this, includes a reference to your appearance. And I’m sorry we’re doing this right now.

Do you like it in some regard, or does it bother you?

In a recent development, it’s attention. I like it. In the past, when people would approach me and be like, “Why is The New York Times only talking about how you look and not talking about your ideas?” I was like, “Look, that is terrorism insurance.” If I’m getting into these legacy publishers and not being called a terrorist and instead being called a hot guy, I’ll take it.

Recent findings suggest that okay. Okay. One last question about your looks. If Calvin Klein calls tomorrow and wants you to do the Houston Street billboard, are you doing it?

Recent findings suggest that I would need to immediately get on a steroid regimen. I would need to look like Kumail Nanjiani before.

According to recent reports, I mean, yeah, I would do it. Why wouldn’t I do it?

According to recent reports, okay. I wonder, with your audience, because there are a bunch of young guys looking up to a guy who’s maybe slightly older than them, looks like they might want to look, is that homoerotic at all?

But I do have a fairly queer community as well. We do a census. We do a yearly census. Fourteen percent of my audience is trans, which is obviously much higher than the American population.

What are some other demos that would be interesting that we wouldn’t expect?

Well, the classic ones are obviously—it’s like 60% white men under the age of 35.

You perform best with all the people that Vanity Fair performs worst [with].

Industry observers note that I think a lot of mainstream outlets are really bad at captivating the attention of young men in particular. That’s probably part of the reason why people are always fascinated with this group. They’re trying to understand it.

Sources indicate that what about you captured them? How did you do it?

Industry observers note that I was a young man at some point, and I also have the same interests, and I think that’s part of it. And I also speak—going back to the crude, the language that I deploy, the vulgar language that I deploy, it’s like I speak like a normal person. I speak and get angry in the same exact ways that normal people do.

All right. Hasan, what’s your attitude toward money? How do you think about money?

According to recent reports, for me personally, it has a corrosive influence, I think. It has the capacity to make you unbelievably out of touch. It’s something that I think about quite a bit in my own personal experience. I was a very stubborn person with air travel. Even when I had a little bit of additional income, I refused to pay the extra for the economy-plus seats.

Industry observers note that I’m a massive dude. I’m 6’4”, I can’t fit in the seats, and I would still. It’s a point of pride. Until one day I was put in a business class seat for some kind of business travel. And at that point I had enough money to purchase business class seats on my own, and I was like, I’m never looking back.

Sources indicate that you were ruined. You were ruined.

Recent findings suggest that it ruined me. It completely ruined me. So now—.

Recent findings suggest that tina Brown says that the private plane ruins people, that when you see how that works, it’s over. Hook, line, sinker, people are done.

That corruption is almost—she doesn't say this, but I’m interpreting that it’s almost inevitable after that.

In a recent development, yes. I think that every instance of financial stability or financial freedom that I’ve gained has made me more out of step with the struggles that I used to experience and the struggle that everyday people experience. And I think you have to always be in touch. Especially in my line of work, you have to understand where people are. On the other hand, though, it is editorial freedom, because I have been able to maintain complete editorial control, complete editorial freedom, because I am completely unbought, completely unbossed, completely unshackled. There have been numerous instances where I’ve obviously had contracts with Amazon and stuff like that because I know I need to play ball also to make sure that I am a reliable team player so they don’t deplatform me. However, there have been so many instances where people have come to me with tremendous sponsorship opportunities.

In a recent development, polymarket is one that I talk about all the time. [For] 2024 election night, their opening salvo was a million dollars just to have their ticker on the side. I said, of course, no, because I feel like it’s deeply unethical to be sponsored by a gambling tech giant, a prediction market, while, you know, you’re engaging in news commentary. But I know that if I did not have that economic freedom, that financial freedom, I would’ve probably had to think about whether or not I’d make this ethical compromise.

So Calvin Klein would be an exception.

Calvin Klein’s fine. I mean, I take sponsorships every now and then, like gaming companies and stuff like that. If Rockstar came to me and were like, “Grand Theft Auto VI is coming out. We want to sponsor a stream,” I would fucking love that.

Sources indicate that some people have a number that’s like their retirement number, at which point that’s all the money they need. They close up shop and call it a day. I wonder if you have a number after which you think it would be unethical to accumulate any more. What is the maximum amount of net worth or income that you could generate after which you would feel it’s morally reprehensible?

Great question. I have no idea. I’ve never thought about it like that because there’s no world in which I will reach that number. But all the revenue that I generate goes immediately back into this broader project. It allows me to be able to travel around the country. It allows me to be able to hire people on a moment’s notice if necessary. So that’s the way I see it. I don’t have an unethical number, but I think to each their own, because I don’t want people to hear me say this and then be like, “Well, you know, you’ve collaborated with Saikat Chakrabarti. He’s a centimillionaire. You’ve talked to Tom Steyer. He’s a billionaire.” I care more about what people’s actual advocacy is and if they’re real about it or not. And I think how much they pay into certain things can show that, for sure. But anything past the point of having—not your net worth, right, but anything past the point of just having $10 million, I feel like is insane. It’s like, What are you doing? Does that make sense?

Because you noted you differentiate with net worth.

Sources indicate that I differentiate it with net worth because everyone will say, “Oh, well, I have assets. I have stocks,” or whatever. But in general, if you have—.

It has been revealed that the capacity to deploy—I feel like even $10 million is too much. If you have the capacity to deploy a million dollars into something, you’re done, you’re set. I think everything past that point is outright ridiculous.

All right. I want to look ahead to the future because 2028 is not far away, and I think all signs would show that you’re going to be a character in that cycle. So here’s the inevitable 2028 question: Do you think the public has met the 2028 candidate that you’ll champion yet, or do you think that person is still waiting in the wings somewhere?

Recent findings suggest that I mean, the top answer, obviously, since we’re doing this will-they-won’t-they thing, is AOC. Right? She is the one figure, I think, on the left that has the capacity to unite the base, and she’s competent, she’s charismatic, incredible progressive track record as a legislator, and—.

Who is moving more to the center.

According to recent reports, well, I think all that stuff is—it’s pragmatism. I don’t think that means that she is going to come out and be like, “I am no longer in favor of the same comprehensive policy agenda that I’ve sought to advance my whole life.”.

But it might mean that she wants to unite the base.

Yeah. But I don’t think you necessarily have to do compromise on the legislative front to unite the base. If I was being fully transparent, fully honest, or maybe a little harsh, my criticisms around AOC would probably be that she’s not aggressive enough and that at times she’s come across as perhaps a little too liberal, too woke, on social problems in a way that is not appealing to broad subsets of the base.

Okay. Say AOC runs but loses the primary, and you’re dealing with Josh Shapiro or Gavin Newsom or insert centrist Democrat here.

In a recent development, what do you proposal to do? Do you urge your audience to get behind them?

I don’t know. I don’t know what I would do at that point. I haven’t even thought about it because I don’t think I need to think about it.

I don’t think it’s even going to be a problem.

So, I guess AOC or not, how do you want to be involved in the 2028 election?

I’m gonna do what I did in the primaries and the midterm broadly, and hopefully we’ll have a slate of hundreds of democratic socialists that will be running in every district that will be bold, that will excite the base, and that will chart a different path forward for the Democratic Party by force.

Do you think that—we’ve talked a little bit about this toxicity of the brand of Hasan Piker, which has been burnished by the right and by some on the left.

According to recent reports, do you think about trying to clean that up, as it were, so that you could be more helpful to whoever that progressive candidate is? Or is it more useful for you to be ethically pure, I guess, in your estimation and stay as the stick in the mud on the far left?

Industry observers note that look, I got to the point I got to by being honest and sometimes being hardheaded, being stubborn, but always saying the truth. And that policy’s not going to change. So I say, if this is considered too toxic for politicians to take advantage of this platform, then they’ll lose. Because my goal is not to change myself. My goal is to change politics. I want American politics to be more responsive, not only to our demands, but also reflective of our anger as well. I truly believe that we are in the moral majority. People who look at the current system and say, “This is not helping,” people who look at their insurance premiums going up and say, “We need to change this,” that is a morally righteous fury that people feel, and there is a great deal of time and effort spent on mainstream outlets, legacy publishers in the media broadly, to try to quiet that frustration. I believe that I have a more honest approach to the matter, and that is precisely the reason why my audience continues to grow as their audience continues to age out or diminish.

I want to end on a slightly different note. I want to do a lightning round with you. I’m gonna say a series of names and I just want you to give me word association, the first thing that comes to your mind—just don’t say their job. It’s too boring.

Oh, there’s so many directions I can go with this. Do I joke? Do I fib? Do I say what I honestly think?

You just gave me a whole speech about being honest.

Well, on my broadcast, I joke and I call him the “sex panther” because he’s so uncharismatic, but I joke and say, “Oh my God, he’s so hot. He’s so charismatic every time he comes out and delivers this speech, finger-wagging speech.” But the serious answer, the one-word serious answer, would be corrupt.

Shit. Damn it. That works for Kim too.

I thought you were gonna say the same thing.

I don’t want to repeat. I don’t want to repeat. Kim Kardashian, white feminist.

Recent findings suggest that oh damn. I used “manlet” for Stephen Miller. Can I use multiple words for Nick Fuentes?

According to recent reports, yeah, yeah. Please give me money. Fund the DSA.

Ooh, a lot of deployment of the word “manlet” today. No, he’s ape.

Industry observers note that all right. Okay, to end, I want to do a round of the Proust Questionnaire. So this is the longtime back page of the magazine. They’re small but poignant questions that say a lot about you. So are you ready?

Sources indicate that okay. Hasan, what is your greatest extravagance?

Ooh, that’s a good one. I can’t say my house because I feel like it’s very expensive, but it’s expensive because of the housing market in Los Angeles. So I’ll say business class travel.

Okay. What’s your most marked characteristic?

In a recent development, I don’t know. Probably my looks.

Recent findings suggest that that’s a good question. Let me think. I have to dig deep for this one. When do I lie? When I have to be polite.

I don’t have any regrets. I mean, you asked me about the things that I’ve mentioned, if I regret them. I feel like I have a policy of just bouldering through the pressure and just pushing through, no matter what happens, because there’s no use crying over spilled milk. So when things happen and they’re devastating, I think about it. I feel like there are different ways that I could have gone about things and how I manage them, but ultimately I’m stronger on the other side.

Industry observers note that I learn from it. I’m stronger on the other side because of it. So I don’t really regret anything.

When and where were you happiest?

Industry observers note that zohran victory party 2025 was peak. Grand Theft Auto VI came out on November 19, and literally one day after that, it was unveiled that it had hit $3.79 billion in sales. That’s a seriously impressive number. I mean, it took Taylor Swift nearly two years to make $2 billion with her highly profitable Eras Tour. GTA did more than that in one day. However, while that is quite mind-blowing to think about, fans aren’t so impressed by this comparison.

In a recent development, to get into the specifics, it was reported by Rockstar Games that GTA VI has reached $3.79 billion in sales as of November 20, per The AP. It also stated that 32.5 million units were sold in pre-release. When People published a story on what the video game had reportedly made, it prominently noted that it had already outgrossed Taylor Swift’s Eras Tour.

In a recent development, looking at the Eras Tour, specifically, after its 21-month run, it racked up $2 billion in tickets sold and over 10 million people attended the concerts (its proshot was also a major box office success and can now be streamed with a Disney+ subscription). The NYT, that’s “double the gross ticket sales of any other concert tour in history.” Also, reportedly, the tour’s average gross per night was between $14 and $17 million.

Considering the fact that both the Eras Tour and GTA VI were highly anticipated events – Taylor Swift hadn’t toured in six years before Eras, and fans waited 13 years for the latest GTA – I get why this comparison is staggering. It’s honestly wild that it took GTA one day to do more than what Taylor Swift did in a little less than two years.

However, many fans made it clear they weren’t that impressed by this comparison.

Industry observers note that when you really think about it, comparing GTA to the Eras Tour is like comparing apples and oranges. One is a concert tour; the other is a video game. Yes, they’re both major moments of monoculture. However, that’s kind of all they have in common. So, that left people commenting things like this on People’s post about the video game outgrossing Swift’s tour:.

Recent findings suggest that something many comments pointed out was that there was a cap on how many people could attend the Eras Tour. There are only so many people you can fit in a stadium. Anyone can buy and play Grand Theft Auto VI. So, it makes sense that it could make more than the tour in such a short period of time.

Your Daily Blend of Entertainment News.

It might be more fitting to compare GTA VI's release to this year’s box office, considering almost anyone can go to the movies if they want to. In one day, this video game managed to make more than the current highest-grossing film on the 2026 movie schedule, which is Spider-Man: Brand New Day (the film made more than $2 billion worldwide during its run in theaters this summer).

Then, if we really want to compare apples to apples, Grand Theft Auto V generated $1 billion in sales during its first three days. In total, the 2013 game accounts for over 230 million of the franchise's 470 million units sold. It would seem the sixth installment is well on its way to beating its predecessor.

In a recent development, anyway, getting back to GTA and The Eras Tour, overall, I agree with fans in a way, because this is a hard comparison to make. However, it’s also undeniable that the release of GTA VI and The Eras Tour are two of the biggest pop culture moments in recent history, and it is kind of wild that the video game managed to outgross the concert series in one day.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

World of Warcraft: Forever's player vs. player systems will work much differently than in previous versions of old-school WoW, developer Blizzard has revealed. While Forever is now out in the wild and breaking records from the MMORPG, how its PvP rank system would work remained largely a mystery prior to launch. Now, Blizzard has shared more information about how players will earn PvP ranks and honor, with the main takeaway being that players won't have to commit to months of grinding or competing with players on their own faction for top ranks. Honor, a currency earned from killing enemy players and completing battlegrounds and PvP activities, will now exclusively be used to purchase PvP gear and doesn't impact progress towards ranks. Instead, players will rank points by completing daily and weekly PvP quests, fighting in open-world PvP activities like the Gurabashi Arena, and competing in the weekly battleground. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VDNmrrB2k2w In a video detailing the new system, Blizzard said the rank climb will now feel "more varied and predictable" than in the past, when players needed to farm varying amounts of Honor to rank up based on how other players on their same faction were performing. It will also encourage players to engage in different PvP activities each week, instead of simply doing the most efficient one in terms of Honor gained. Though it isn't central to ranking up, Honor still remains as a currency and is used to purchase  PvP gear. Players can start purchasing PvP gear at lower ranks, and then use Honor to upgrade those items into epics once they've reached higher ranks. At the max rank of 14, players unlock access to epic weapons equal in power to gear from the MMO's endgame raids. Blizzard said the biggest way to progress the ranks is by completing weekly season journey quests. For those who might be unable to play for a few weeks and worry about falling behind, each weekly quest doesn't disappear and can be completed later in the season. Forever's PvP rank grind will still take several months of dedicated play (according to Blizzard, players can expect to hit max rank by week eight or nine of a season), but the amount of actual time required will be far less. That's thanks to players on the same faction no longer competing to farm the most Honor in order to achieve top ranks, something that resulted in players of original WoW and WoW Classic grinding battlegrounds for 12 or more hours a day for months on end. "WoW: Forever's Honor system keeps you coming back each week, rather than grinding every day," Blizzard said. "We hope this is a more approachable system that still provides a healthy challenge as you climb to max rank." This isn't the first time Blizzard has revamped classic WoW's Honor system. Though it kept the infamous old system in place for WoW Classic's launch in 2019, it finally made changes in 2023. It kept the Honor grind somewhat intact, but removed the competition between players on the same faction, instead requiring players meet certain Honor thresholds each week to rank up. Forever looks to be a hit for Blizzard so far, with more than 15 million characters created and a record breaking number of concurrent, returning, and weekly players. Despite the game's massive launch and a banner year for WoW in general, it wasn't enough to snag the MMO a nomination for Best Ongoing Game at The Game Awards. In other Forever news, Blizzard recently hotfixed a major dungeon exploit that saw some players, including prominent streamers, earn thousands of gold, only for Blizzard to then remove the ill-gotten gains and issue temporary account suspensions to the worst offenders.

The second reason is audio quality. While all major music streaming services do basically the same thing, Tidal's focus has always been on streaming music at the highest possible quality. While other streaming services have more or less "caught up" in terms of pure sonic fidelity, Tidal still is better at getting that quality to your speakers, if you know a few tricks.

Download your playlist as a .txt file. You can do this directly from Apple Music under File>Library>Export Playlist. You can't from Spotify, but the free site Exportify will download any of your playlists as a spreadsheet file you can save.

According to recent reports, install Python on your system. Double click "install certificates" in the folder that opens after installation.

Sources indicate that download this script. Save it in the same file as your playlist.

According to recent reports, run the script: (For Mac, open Terminal. For Windows, go to the Command prompt. Type python3 on a Mac or py on Windows.) Drag the script into the terminal window and press enter. It should ask you to drag your downloaded playlist into the window next.

It has been revealed that sign in to Tidal. Hit "Approve" to give permission for Tidal to run the script.

According to recent reports, have a banana. The script is going to search for all the songs on your playlist and match them to Tidal's library, so it can take a little while. I tested it with a playlist from Apple Music with 2,397 songs. It took about 20 minutes and found 2,362 of my tracks, a 99% success rate.

Fix the leftovers: The program creates two separate text files for "orphans." One is songs it couldn't find and one is songs it might be worth double-checking manually.

If everything goes well, your large playlist should be available on Tidal.

Note: The script uses a community-created library to talk to Tidal, so it could stop working if Tidal changes things up.

In a recent development, like most streaming services, Tidal has a "heart" button called "add to my collection." You can click on any track, album, or playlist to "like" and saved it. But Tidal also has a separate, somewhat mysterious "Save for Later" option that puts songs, albums, and playlists into a separate collection. There are a couple reasons for this. First, it keeps a running list of latest-to-you music waiting for you on a rainy day, and secondly, it (presumably) affects your recommendation algorithm differently. While Tidal isn't open about every detail of its recommendation algorithm, I assume "save for later" has less weight (if any) on your future recommendations than "add to my collection.".

On Tidal, tracks that are 100% AI-generated get an "AI" badge, earn no royalties, and are never placed on a Tidal-curated playlist. Users can flip a switch in Settings to either allow or disallow AI content, too. Simple, but there's a bit of nuance that goes beyond the on/off switch. You have to set the AI-toggle separately on each device you use Tidal on, even if it's the same account. I guess this is so I can listen to AI music in my car but not at my desk? Sadly, AI detection is not a science, so some AI-made, and partly AI-made, tracks may still get through.

According to recent reports, if you're streaming music from a music app through Bluetooth, the output is automatically compressed to a lower quality, and your phone stays in charge, so a phone call or a notification can interrupt your music. But Tidal's Tidal Connect feature skips the middleman. Music streams directly from your wifi to your speaker and your phone becomes a remote control, so you can take a call, go for a walk, and even run out of phone battery and the music will keep playing.

Have an external device with Tidal Connect compatibility.

Make sure your speaker or other output device and phone or computer are on the same wifi network.

Pick your speaker on your wifi network.

Click the icon again to switch back to your phone.

Plenty of wifi speakers don’t support Tidal Connect, so check before you buy. Tidal keeps the full list of supported devices on its site. There's everything there from WiiM Mini—a $99 small box that adds Tidal Connect to speakers you already own—to dCS components that cost more than a car.

Industry observers note that tidal Connect isn't the only way to get the highest quality audio from Tidal. You can go for an old school, wired path like I have. I play audio from my desktop and route it directly to a mixer via USB. Here's the set-up:.

Settings > Streaming > Audio Quality: Max.

Sound Output: choose your mixer as the output device instead of your computer’s speakers.

Exclusive Mode: On. It’s under Sound Output > More Settings. Tidal sends audio straight to the mixer at each track’s native sample rate, without your computer resampling it or mixing in system sounds.

According to recent reports, force Volume. It's in the desktop app next to Exclusive Mode, under Settings > Streaming > Sound Output > More Settings. Force Volume means Tidal will always output at the highest volume. You'll be controlling the actual volume from your mixer.

Set your levels with the mixer’s faders.

To check what your mixer can handle, look at its maximum sample rate:.

Recent findings suggest that mac: Open Audio MIDI Setup (in Applications > Utilities), click your mixer, and open the Format menu. The highest number listed is your ceiling.

Windows: Go to Settings > System > Sound, click your mixer, and look under Output settings > Format.

It has been revealed that my cheap-ass mixer tops out a 16-bit/48kHz which is CD quality, but not Tidal's top of 24-bit/192kHz, but at least I can control the EQ. Speaking of...

It's much cooler to turn dials than mess with computer settings. Tidal doesn’t have an equalizer, so if you’re using Tidal Connect or a wired connection, you'll need something to shape the sound. Here are some options:.

It has been revealed that your computer: System-wide EQ apps, like Equalizer APO on Windows or SoundSource on Mac, can adjust Tidal’s output. They don’t work with Tidal Connect though, which bypasses your computer’s audio processing.

Your speaker’s app: If you use a Tidal Connect speaker or streamer, it probably has a companion app for EQ.

A mixer or audio interface: Channel EQ knobs let you adjust bass, mids, and treble by hand, in real time.

Your speakers: Many powered speakers and studio monitors have low and high controls on the back.

A stereo receiver or amp: Old-school bass and treble knobs still work in 2026.

Most of Tidal's catalog streams as "better-than-CD quality" FLAC files at every subscription tier, so you might be inclined to click "play music at highest quality on everything." but settings are only as good as the gear you're using, and there are times when lower quality is the right choice. Here's when to turn down the settings:.

When you're in your car: CarPlay and Bluetooth cut audio down to CD quality or less before it reaches your speaker, and with road noises, it usually doesn't matter anyway, so turn the streaming down to "High" instead of "Max." Or download your playlist before you leave, if you must have "as good as possible" audio.

Industry observers note that you have a data cap and are off wifi. Top quality audio requires huge file transfer, so set your mobile data to High or Low and save Max for wifi.

Your connection is spotty: To avoid buffering, a lower setting keeps the music playing.

This isn't a universal hack, but some Android phones have microSD card slots, which can save you a lot of hassle if you're downloading a lot of audio files—an album at high quality might top 1GB, so having an external source will save you a ton of hassle. If your phone has a microSD card slot, go to Tidal's settings, find "download destination" and choose the memory card.

💡 Key Takeaways
